cursedLore:
**Lore.** Each of these was a good idea somewhere else, which is the point. Shell sort is
Donald Shell's (1959). Heapsort is J. W. J. Williams' (1964), soon improved by Robert Floyd.
Pancake sorting was posed in 1975 in the American Mathematical Monthly
under the pen name "Harry Dweighter"; its first paper (1979) is the best-known research paper
Bill Gates co-wrote. Counting sort and sorting networks came from 1950s machine design.
Merge insertion is Ford and Johnson's (1959); smoothsort is Dijkstra's (1981). All of them
assume you can reach any position cheaply, which a stack cannot.

hardcoded-three.name: Hardcoded Three
hardcoded-three.doc:
| class | n | ops | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(1) · ✓ | 3 | ≤ 2 | 2 | 2 | ~20 | Common |

**How it plays.** There are 3! = 6 orders. If the max is on top, `ra`. If the max is in the
middle, `rra`. Then, if the top two are out of order, `sa`. This is always optimal for 3
(checked against the Oracle on all 6 orders, sim).

**Lore.** Nothing to tell: with 6 orders, every push_swap writer works the cases out by hand.

**Pros**
- Optimal and trivial to write.
- Used as the finisher in Turk, Min Extract and many others.

**Cons**
- Only for 3. It does not generalise.

**Slots:** none. **Plays as:** Finisher.

five-hand.name: Five Hand
five-hand.tagline: Push the two smallest, fix three, pull back
five-hand.doc:
| class | n | ops | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(1) · ✓ | 4–5 | ≤ 10 (mean 7.4 at n=5) | 2 | 4 | ~40 | Common |

**How it plays.** Rotate the minimum to the top by the shorter way and `pb`. Repeat for the
second minimum. Hardcoded Three on A, then `pa pa`.

**Lore.** Folk 42 knowledge, passed between peers because evaluators used to check 5 values in
≤ 12 ops.

**Pros**
- Simple and reliable. Its worst case at n=5 is 10 ops, so it always fits the common
  "5 values in ≤ 12" bar.

**Cons**
- Not optimal. At n=5 the Oracle needs 2.5 fewer ops on average and up to 6 fewer, and Five
  Hand is optimal on only 7 of the 120 orders (sim). The gap is shown in Lab › Optimality
  gap.

**Slots:** none. **Finisher:** its inner Three (Hardcoded Three by default) can be swapped.
**Plays as:** Finisher for leaves of 5.

oracle.name: Oracle
oracle.doc:
| class | n | ops | Grasp | Craft | Lines | Speed | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| exponential · ✓ optimal | ≤ 8 (BFS), 9+ (IDA*) | optimal | 4 | 6 | ~200 | ●●○○○ | Rare |

**How it plays.** Breadth-first search over states (A, B) using the 11 ops. The first time the
sorted state is reached, the path is the shortest stream. Every way to split an order of the n
values between the two stacks is a state: (n+1)·n! in all. That is 40,320 at n=7, 362,880 at
n=8 (a full BFS takes about a second in Node, sim) and 3.6 million at n=9. Pack each state into
an integer key and keep a visited set. One backward BFS from the sorted state gives the
optimum of every input at once.

**Variants.** These are params, not technique cards: they change CPU time and the reachable n,
never the op count.
- **Bidirectional BFS:** search from both ends and meet in the middle, roughly a square-root
  saving in states.
- **IDA\*:** iterative deepening with an admissible heuristic, so memory stays flat and n ≥ 9
  becomes feasible. Inversions ÷ 2 is **not** admissible: `[1 2 3 4 0]` scores 2 but is one
  `rra` from sorted. A safe one: read A followed by B reversed as a cycle. `pa` and `pb` never
  change that cycle, and one op removes at most 5 **breakpoints** (neighbours that are not
  consecutive ranks), so max(|B|, ⌈breakpoints ÷ 5⌉) never overestimates (checked on every
  state up to n=8, sim). It is weak, about a fifth of the true distance, so a pattern database
  is the real upgrade.
- **Distance tables:** precompute a backward BFS from the goal once, then look up any small
  leaf in O(1).
- **Op pruning:** never play an op right after its inverse, and never `ra` then `rb` when `rr`
  exists.

**Lore.** Breadth-first search was reinvented by Edward F. Moore in 1959 to find the shortest
way out of a maze (Konrad Zuse had it in 1945, unpublished until 1972). IDA* is Richard Korf's
1985 answer to BFS's memory hunger, tested on the 15-puzzle, which is exactly the kind of
problem a small push_swap is.

**Pros**
- Ground truth. Every heuristic's optimality gap is measured against it.
- As a leaf solver inside quicksorts, it saves a measurable number of ops.

**Cons**
- Exponential: 3.6 million states at n=9 and 40 million at n=10. Beyond ~9 values it needs
  serious engineering.
- C needs a hash set and a queue (malloc-heavy, so watch the leaks).

**Slots:** none; the variants above are params. **Plays as:** Finisher (BFS Leaf) and as the
baseline in the Lab.

bubble-wheel.name: Bubble Wheel
bubble-wheel.tagline: Turn the wheel, swap when wrong
bubble-wheel.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 11301 sim FAIL | 301410 sim FAIL | 2 | 2 | ~25 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** Bubble sort using only A. Each pass does, n−1 times: if the top two are out of
order, `sa`; then `ra`. One more `ra` completes the revolution. Repeat the pass until A is
sorted. B is never used.

**Lore.** Bubble sort was first described by Edward Friend in 1956 as "sorting by exchange".
Kenneth Iverson seems to have named it "bubble sort" in 1962. It survives as the first sort
people are taught, not because anyone uses it. Knuth's verdict: it "seems to have nothing to
recommend it, except a catchy name and the fact that it leads to some interesting theoretical
problems". Here it shows why a single swap op is weak.

**Pros**
- The purest illustration of the op set: it shows why `sa` alone is weak and why B exists.
- Very short.

**Cons**
- About n² ops, which fails both grades badly.

**Slots:** none. Stopping as soon as A is sorted is built in, and the measured count
includes it.
**Teaching role:** the first card of the Path. It shows the problem every later card solves.

min-extract.name: Min Extract
min-extract.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 1454 sim GOOD | 32298 sim FAIL | 2 | 2 | ~40 | Common |

**How it plays.** Find the minimum of A, rotate it to the top by the shorter direction, `pb`.
Repeat until 3 remain, finish with Hardcoded Three (with only 2 values, `sa` if needed), then
`pa` everything back. B ends in descending order from the top, so the `pa`s rebuild A in
order.

**Lore.** Plain selection sort: the way anyone sorts a hand of cards by picking out the
smallest each time. No inventor to credit.

**Pros**
- Easy to prove: each extraction costs at most n/2 rotations plus 1.
- A very common choice for the subject's O(n²) "simple" slot.
- Doubles as the Five Hand.

**Cons**
- Each rotation passes over values without doing anything useful with them.
- It fails n=500.

**Slots:** none. Keep Three is native, and the Finisher is Hardcoded Three by default.
Presorted Shortcut is a prep card, so it fits without a slot.

twin-extract.name: Twin Extract
twin-extract.tagline: Smallest or largest, whichever is closer
twin-extract.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 1117 sim GOOD | 22318 sim FAIL | 4 | 4 | ~80 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** At each step, find the cheaper of the current min and the current max to bring
to the top. A min goes `pb` onto the top of B. A max goes `pb` then `rb` to the bottom of B.
At the end, B holds the mins (descending from the top) above the maxes, and the maxes run
from the largest down to the smallest. Return the mins with `pa`. The largest max is now on
B's top, so `pa` the maxes one by one, then rotate that block of maxes to the bottom of A
(`ra`, or `rra` if shorter).

**Lore.** Double-ended selection (min and max at once) is a classic textbook tweak. Nothing
more to it.

**Pros**
- Cuts the average search distance by about a third compared with Min Extract: 8.6 against
  13.0 rotations per extraction at n=100 (sim). The closer of two random positions in a stack
  of m is about m/6 away, against m/4 for one.
- A natural "first optimisation" exercise.

**Cons**
- The return phase is easy to get wrong. The obvious `rrb` + `pa` per max brings the maxes
  back upside down: it sorted 0 of 1000 inputs (sim).
- Still O(n²), and still fails n=500.

**Slots:** none. A Finisher is optional, for example Hardcoded Three for the last 3.
Presorted Shortcut is a prep card, so it fits without a slot.

insert-into-b.name: Insert-into-B
insert-into-b.tagline: Keep B sorted as you go
insert-into-b.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 1459 sim GOOD | 32251 sim FAIL | 4 | 4 | ~90 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** Take A's top, rotate B (the shorter way) until the slot for that value is on
top, then `pb`. B stays circularly sorted in descending order. At the end, rotate B's max to
the top and `pa` everything.

**Lore.** Plain insertion sort, as when you slide each new card into place in your hand. The
twist here is the circular slot.

**Pros**
- It introduces the circular slot, the core idea of the whole family.

**Cons**
- It never chooses *which* value to insert, so it pays for every unlucky one.
- About the same count as Min Extract.

**Slots:** 2, from anchor (mirrored, with a caveat), pick and cost.

simple-insertion.name: Simple Insertion
simple-insertion.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 1462 sim GOOD | 32242 sim FAIL | 4 | 4 | ~100 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** `pb` everything. Then repeatedly take B's top, rotate A to its slot, and `pa`.
Finish by rotating A's minimum to the top.

**Lore.** Same idea as Insert-into-B, mirrored. No separate history.

**Pros**
- This is the base that every Insertion technique plugs into. It is the cleanest card for
  measuring what each technique is worth.

**Cons**
- It pushes values that were already in a good order.
- It takes values blindly from B's top.

**Slots:** 4, from anchor, pick, cost, band and order. With Quick 2-Way, it has the most
slots of any card. It is the main **lab bench** for Insertion techniques.

lis-insertion.name: LIS Insertion
lis-insertion.tagline: Keep the longest ordered line, insert the rest
lis-insertion.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 547 sim EXC | 5059 sim EXC | 6 | 6 | ~300 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Find a longest increasing subsequence (patience sorting, O(n log n)). Pass 1:
`ra` past values on the LIS and `pb` the rest, so A becomes the LIS in circular order. Pass 2:
insert each value of B back, choosing the cheapest value in B, with A and B rotating together
(`rr`/`rrr`) when their directions agree. Final rotation of the minimum to the top.

The numbers above are the bare card, with its default Two-Way Cost. The Long Line deck adds
Four-Way Cost and `rb` Sink and measures 530 / 4425 (sim).

**Lore.** Patience sorting is named after the solitaire card game. Colin Mallows named it,
crediting A. S. C. Ross with inventing it in the early 1960s, and in 1973 Mallows noted that
the number of piles equals the longest increasing subsequence. In 1977 Logan–Shepp and
Vershik–Kerov independently proved that the LIS of a random permutation grows like 2√n. That is
why the anchor keeps only about 17 of 100 values.

**Pros**
- One of the strongest O(n²) cards. It is EXCELLENT at both sizes, on every sim run.
- It pushes the fewest values possible for a non-circular anchor: n − LIS. The LIS is about
  17 values at n=100 and 40 at n=500 (sim).
- Easy to justify in a README.

**Cons**
- Patience sorting with predecessor links is a new idea for most peers.
- The worst-case bound is quadratic, so it cannot serve as the subject's O(n log n) method.

**Slots:** 3 (cost, band, order). LIS Anchor and Cheapest Pick are native. The cost role
starts as Two-Way Cost.

turk.name: Turk
turk.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²) · ✓ | 557 sim EXC | 5088 sim EXC | 4 | 6 | ~250 | Common |

**How it plays.** This is the most popular 42 push_swap ("Mechanical Turk", credited to a 42
student; see sources). Start with `pb pb`. While A has more than 3 values: for **every** value
in A, find its target in B (the largest smaller value, or B's max) and price the four rotation
combinations (`rr`, `rrr`, `ra+rrb`, `rra+rb`); perform the cheapest and `pb`. Finish the last
3 with Hardcoded Three. Then return each top of B to its slot in A (the smallest larger value,
or A's min) and rotate the min to the top.

**Lore.** A 42-peer invention, popularised by a 2023 Medium post (see sources). The name comes
from the Mechanical Turk, the 1770 chess automaton that hid a human player inside: the
algorithm looks clever, but it is a brute-force check of every move. The intuition to keep:
price every option, take the cheapest, repeat.

**Pros**
- EXCELLENT on every sim run at both sizes: at n=500 the mean is 5088 and the worst of 200
  runs is 5466 (sim). Web reports range from 5100 to 6500 at n=500, depending on details.
- Easy to explain with a picture.
- Many peer write-ups exist.

**Cons**
- There are many fiddly details: targets, four cost cases, the empty-B start. Debugging is the
  main cost.
- It pushes **everything**, including values that were already in good order (compare LIS
  Insertion).
- O(n²) CPU per move (about 65 ms per sort at n=500 in the sim's JS) is fine at 500 but slow
  beyond.
- Labelling it O(n log n) is a common mistake: one insertion can cost |A|/2 + |B|/2, and the
  measured ops ÷ n log₂ n keep rising: 0.87 at n=128, 1.69 at n=2048 (sim), 2.25 at n=5000
  (ref).

**Slots:** 3, from anchor, cost, band and order. Cheapest Pick is native. Keep Three (anchor)
and Four-Way Cost (cost) are defaults, and Hardcoded Three is the default Finisher.

chunks.name: Chunks
chunks.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n√n) · ~ (✓ with K ∝ √n and One-Way Sweep) | 662 sim EXC | 5927 sim GOOD | 4 | 4 | ~150 | Common |

**How it plays.** Split the ranks into K chunks (the sim uses K = round(√n / 2): 5 chunks at
n=100 and 11 at n=500). For each chunk in order: bring its nearest member in A to the top (by
either direction) and `pb`. If the value is in the lower half of its chunk, also `rb` (a
"sink"), so B forms an hourglass. When A is empty, repeatedly bring B's max to the top and
`pa`.

**Lore.** Bucket sort's idea (split by range, then order within each range) dates from the
punched-card era. In push_swap it is folk 42 knowledge, usually the first 'medium' method peers
find.

**Pros**
- Intuitive and easy to visualise.
- EXCELLENT at n=100 on average, though 5 % of runs reach 700 or more (sim).
- The upgrade path is short and measured. One-Way Sweep is both cheaper and provable (−16 at
  n=100, −140 at n=500), Second-Max saves 26 / 385, and K ≈ 0.4√n is the best chunk count.
  Together they make the Crate Runner deck: 606 / 5247, EXCELLENT on every run (sim).

**Cons**
- Sensitive to the chunk count, but tuning alone does not reach EXCELLENT at n=500: the best
  K is 9, at 5858 (sim). Web write-ups report ~4900–5035 at n=500 with retrieval tricks this
  card's defaults lack.
- Max retrieval rescans B every time. That is fine for ops, but O(n²) CPU.
- A constant chunk count (not ∝ √n) quietly breaks the O(n√n) claim. So does the default
  Nearest-Member Sweep, which can pass the same value many times.

**Slots:** 3, from anchor (with a caveat), sweep, band, retrieval and order. Defaults:
Nearest-Member Sweep, `rb` Sink and Max Retrieval, which are what the measured numbers use.
Param: the chunk count K.

butterfly.name: Butterfly
butterfly.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n√n) · ✕ with a constant w; ✓ with w = k·√n | 577 sim EXC | 5080 sim EXC | 4 | 4 | ~80 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** Keep a counter i of how many values have been pushed so far. For A's top x:
if rank(x) ≤ i, then `pb` + `rb` (sink it); else if rank(x) ≤ i + w, then `pb`; otherwise
`ra`. This produces a "butterfly" shape in B. Then retrieve the max of B repeatedly. The sim
uses w = 15 at n=100 and w = 30 above, like one reference build, which makes w a constant
beyond n=100. With w = round(1.4√n) instead (14 and 31), it measures the same at the grading
sizes, 577 / 5077, and keeps its class (sim).

**Lore.** A folk 42 name for the shape B takes: low values sunk to the bottom, high ones on
top, like two wings. No published origin.

**Pros**
- Very short code for its strength. It beats Chunks at both sizes in the sim.
- No chunk bookkeeping.

**Cons**
- With a constant w, the cost per value grows with n, so claiming O(n√n) is wrong unless w
  scales with √n. The grading sizes hide it: ops ÷ n√n is 0.45 at n=1000 and only climbs
  after, to 0.61 at n=4096 (sim).
- Retrieval is still a blind max search. Second-Max saves 19 at n=100 and 279 at n=500 (sim).

**Slots:** 2, from band and retrieval. The window rule is native: it decides which value is
pushed next and, through its sink, where it lands. Defaults: `rb` Sink (through the window
rule) and Max Retrieval. Param: the window w.

bucket-insertion.name: Bucket Insertion
bucket-insertion.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n√n) · ✓ | 606 sim EXC (576 ref) | 4291 sim EXC (4121 ref) | 6 | 6 | ~300 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Buckets of about c·√n ranks (a reference build uses ⌊4√n⌋), each pushed in a
**One-Way Sweep**, with lower-half sinking. The return is **cheapest insertion restricted to
the current bucket**: pick the member of the highest remaining bucket whose combined A and B
rotation is cheapest, sharing `rr`/`rrr`. Restricting the choice to one bucket keeps the
O(n√n) proof valid.

**Lore.** A recombination rather than an invention: Chunks' buckets plus Turk's cheapest
return, restricted per bucket so the proof survives. One reference build did it this way.

**Pros**
- Takes Turk's cost-based return and gives it a provable O(n√n) bound. This makes a strong
  "medium" method for the subject.
- It is the medium method of one reference build: 576 / 4121 (ref, 5 seeds). The sim's
  version measures 606 / 4291, EXCELLENT on every run. Either way it beats Turk at n=500 with
  a provable class.

**Cons**
- Two phases, each with its own tuning.
- The proof needs care: an unrestricted cheapest pick breaks it.

**Slots:** 3, from sweep, band, cost and order. The bucket-restricted pick and return are
native. Defaults: One-Way Sweep, `rb` Sink and Two-Way Cost. Param: the bucket width.

lsd-radix.name: LSD Radix
lsd-radix.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 1084 sim GOOD | 6784 sim GOOD | 4 | 2 | ~40 | Common |

**How it plays.** Replace values with ranks 0..n−1. For each bit from least to most
significant: walk A once, `pb` if the bit is 0 and `ra` if it is 1, then `pa` everything back.
Every pass costs exactly n + (number of zeros). Passes = ⌈log₂ n⌉.

**Lore.** Radix sort is older than computers. Herman Hollerith's punched-card machines date
from the 1890 US census, and card sorters split a deck one column at a time into ten pockets.
Sorting from the least significant column first was a trick found by machine operators: it was
first written down in 1930 and appears in IBM's earliest known sorter manual (1936). Each pass
is stable, so earlier columns stay in order, and that is exactly this card. Harold Seward
brought radix sort to computers in 1954.

**Pros**
- The shortest real O(n log n) card, and trivially provable.
- **Zero spread**: the count is identical for every random input of the same n. Its 6784 at
  n=500 is exactly the count in the subject's own large-input example.
- The classic first n log n card.
- Peephole Cancel trims 78 ops at n=100 and 55 at n=500 (sim): the run of `pb`s at the end of
  a pass is undone by the `pa`s that follow.

**Cons**
- It never reaches EXCELLENT.
- It ignores existing order completely: a nearly sorted input costs the same as a random one.
- B is only a bucket. No rotation is ever used cleverly.

**Slots:** none: radix never chooses which value to move or where it lands. Param: skip sorted
passes (stop when A is already sorted; this helps only on structured inputs).

**Teaching role:** the Path's first "fast" card. Peers often stop here. The Meta page shows
the gap to EXCELLENT.

ternary-radix.name: Ternary Radix
ternary-radix.tagline: Three-way digits using both ends of B
ternary-radix.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 1333 sim GOOD | 7362 sim GOOD | 6 | 6 | ~150 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Base-3 digits of the rank. Per pass, digit 0 → `pb` + `rb` (bottom of B),
digit 1 → `pb` (top of B), digit 2 → `ra` (stays in A). Then gather the three groups back into
A in digit order with `rrb`/`pa` and `pa`. There are ⌈log₃ n⌉ passes: 5 for n=100 and 6 for
n=500, against 7 and 9 for binary.

**Lore.** Same lineage as LSD Radix, with base 3 instead of 2. Card sorters used base 10, one
pocket per digit; here B's two ends plus A act as three pockets.

**Pros**
- Fewer passes. It uses B's bottom, which binary radix ignores.
- A good bridge to Four-End Quicksort's "four locations" idea.

**Cons**
- Each pass costs more: about 2.3n ops against 1.5n for binary. The values sent to B's bottom
  pay `pb rb` on the way out and `rrb pa` on the way back. As described it measures
  1333 / 7362 (sim), **worse** than binary radix at both sizes. Choosing the cheaper top and
  bottom assignment per pass only gets it to 1115 / 7300 (sim). A gather that skips the
  `rrb` return trip is the open question.
- It still ignores existing order.

**Slots:** none. Param: the gather order, that is, which digit goes to which location.

msd-radix.name: MSD Radix
msd-radix.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 757 sim GOOD | 5263 sim EXC | 6 | 6 | ~200 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** Split the chunk by the top bit of its rank range: values below the
power-of-two cut go to B, the rest stay in A, and each half is sorted recursively, top bit
first. On ranks 0..n−1 this is exactly Quick 2-Way with the pivot moved to a power of two, and
the sim builds it that way: same pushes, same restores, same 2-value leaves.

**Lore.** MSD radix is the other way card sorters could be run: split on the most significant
column first, then sort each pocket separately. It needs a separate pile per pocket, which is
why operators preferred LSD. On stacks, the "piles" are recursion, so MSD turns out to be a
quicksort.

**Pros**
- The subject names it, and it shows that radix and quicksort are cousins.
- Like Quick 2-Way, a sorted chunk costs nothing: sorted input is free.

**Cons**
- A power-of-two cut splits unevenly when the range is not a power of two, so it is a little
  worse than the median: 757 / 5263 against Quick 2-Way's 718 / 5235 (sim).
- It shares Quick 2-Way's restore overhead.

**Slots:** none. A Finisher is optional; by default, leaves of 2 are fixed with `sa`/`sb`.

quick-2way.name: Quick 2-Way
quick-2way.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 718 sim GOOD | 5235 sim EXC | 6 | 6 | ~200 | Uncommon |

**How it plays.** Sort a chunk of k values on top of A by pushing the lower half (below the
median rank) to B and rotating the rest past (`ra`). Then undo those rotations (`rra`) if the
chunk was not the whole stack, recurse on the upper half in A, then do the mirror operation
for the half in B (push the upper part back with `pa`, rotate the rest with `rb`). Leaves of
size 2 are fixed with `sa`/`sb`.

Always restoring the rotations, even when the chunk is the whole stack, would cost 857 / 5967
(sim): the whole-stack case of Restore Skip is part of this card.

**Why the class holds.** Ranks make the median exact, so the recursion depth is ⌈log₂ n⌉. At
each level a value is pushed or rotated at most once, and rotated back at most once by a
restore, so a level costs at most 2 ops per value, plus the leaves. That is O(n log n) in the
worst case. Measured ops stay between 1.0 and 1.35 × n log₂ n on random input up to n=4096
and on reversed and organ-pipe inputs up to n=8192 (sim).

**Lore.** Tony Hoare invented quicksort in 1959 while studying in Moscow. He was working on
machine translation and needed to sort words before looking them up in a dictionary stored on
tape. It was published in 1961 (Algorithm 64, Communications of the ACM) and is still the
default sort in many libraries. The intuition: pick a pivot, split, and never compare across
the split again.

**Pros**
- A real O(n log n) partition method that also uses existing order: a sorted chunk is
  detected and skipped.
- The hardest part is the recursion itself. Once it works, it is compact.

**Cons**
- "Undo the rotations" is pure overhead. It is the main reason this card loses to Four-End
  Quicksort.
- GOOD, not EXCELLENT, at n=100: only 10 % of runs get under 700 (sim). As a build's complex
  method, it costs EXCELLENT on about half of the n=100 runs (see 05-meta, Builds).
- Bugs in the B-side mirror are easy to make.

**Slots:** 4 (ends, split, pivot, order). Defaults: two ends with the rotations restored,
halves, and Median Pivot. A Finisher is optional; by default, leaves of 2 are fixed with
`sa`/`sb`.

four-end-quicksort.name: Four-End Quicksort
four-end-quicksort.tagline: Four bins, never step over anyone
four-end-quicksort.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 735 sim GOOD | 5033 sim EXC | 8 | 8 | ~400 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Treat the tops and bottoms of A and B as **four locations**. A chunk sitting
at one location is split by **exact rank** into three parts, and each part is sent to one of
the other three locations. Every move costs at most 3 ops and never passes over another value,
so nothing is ever "undone". The parts are sorted max first, so sorted values pile up on top
of A; only the max part may be sent there. The bare card has no Finisher: the recursion goes
down to single values. Five Hand cannot serve, because its Hardcoded Three rotates A and would
disturb the sorted values below the leaf. BFS Leaf solves leaves of ≤ 5 optimally around them.

Without a Finisher, its op count depends only on n, not on the order of the input (sim): every
value's path is fixed by its rank. The numbers above are that bare card. With Pivot by Leaf
Count, BFS Leaf ≤ 5 and Peephole, the Four Corners deck, the sim measures 533 / 3825. That
matches the reference build's 528 / 3824, which is that method's own mean over 5 seeds, not
the build's `--adaptive` mean (529.8 / 3948.0).

**Lore.** Three-way partitioning goes back to Dijkstra's 'Dutch national flag' problem (1976):
sort red, white and blue in one pass. Multi-pivot quicksort became mainstream when Java 7
adopted Yaroslavskiy's dual-pivot version in 2011. The four-ends twist is push_swap's own: the
four stack ends are four cheap pockets.

**Pros**
- The strongest provable O(n log n) card in the roster. Bare, it is EXCELLENT at n=500; as
  Four Corners, at both sizes on every run (sim).
- The class has a simple argument: every move costs at most 3 ops and never passes over
  another value, and exact-rank thirds give a depth of about log₃ n. The constant the
  reference build states, ≤ 3n⌈log₃ n⌉ + 13n/5, is its own claim, and the study notes that
  nobody has checked it independently.
- Once the "four locations" model is understood, the code is regular.

**Cons**
- The hardest mental model in the deck: chunks move between ends, and directions flip
  depending on the location.
- Bare, it is only GOOD at n=100 (735). The gains come from its techniques, and they compound:
  BFS Leaf ≤ 5 saves 142 / 657, and Pivot by Leaf Count adds 27 / 334 on top, a synergy (sim).

**Slots:** 3 (split, pivot, order). Four Ends is native. Thirds Split is the default split, and
**DP Splits** replaces it in the Legendary deck (a simplified DP saves 17 / 214 more, sim). The
Finisher slot is empty by default; BFS Leaf is the one to play.

tape-merge.name: Tape Merge
tape-merge.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 1200 exp GOOD | 8100 exp GOOD | 8 | 8 | ~350 | Legendary |

**How it plays.** Treat the four stack ends like the tapes in old **external merge sort**.
First split the input into sorted runs (natural runs, or small runs sorted by a Finisher),
spread across the ends. Then repeatedly merge pairs of runs: compare the heads at two
locations, move the smaller to the output location, and repeat. **Polyphase merge** (a
Fibonacci distribution of runs) reduces the number of passes.

**As built (exp).** A balanced two-way merge in which every value costs one op per merge step.
Each pass starts with all runs ascending on A's top. Distribute: runs alternately go to A's bottom
(`ra`) and to B's top (`pb`), so a run at A's bottom has its largest value lowest and a run on B's
top has its largest value on top. Merge: take the larger head, A's bottom with `rra` or B's top
with `pa`, onto A's top, so each pair becomes one ascending run there and the next pass starts
the same way. A pass costs exactly 2n, and there are ⌈log₂ runs⌉ passes. Random input has
about n/2 natural runs, so the count barely varies: exactly 1200 on every n=100 run, and 8000
or 9000 at n=500 (exp). A Finisher sorts the first runs as blocks: Distance Tables (blocks of 4)
saves 50 / 355, BFS Leaf (blocks of 5) 23 / 215. It beats Natural Merge (1495 / 10165) by not
rotating past the runs it is not merging, but it stays far from Four-End Quicksort. Polyphase
distribution is still open.

**Lore.** John von Neumann wrote a merge routine in 1945 for the EDVAC, among the first
programs written for a stored-program computer. When data lived on magnetic tape, merging runs
between tapes was the way to sort, and polyphase merge (written up by R. L. Gilstad in the
early 1960s) did it with fewer tape drives. Stacks behave much like tapes, which is why this
card exists.

**Pros**
- It uses existing order directly: natural runs make nearly sorted input cheap.
- It is a classic algorithm (Knuth, Vol. 3) that few 42 peers have tried, so there is room
  for new ideas here.

**Cons**
- Every pass touches every value twice (distribute, then merge), so it pays 2n per pass where
  Four-End Quicksort pays at most 3 per value per level of a shallower recursion: 1200 / 8100
  against 735 / 5033 bare (exp).
- It ignores existing order inside the distribution, so a nearly sorted input with a few long
  runs is cheap only when the runs are few.

**Slots:** none. The Finisher is optional and sorts the first runs (BFS Leaf or Distance
Tables). Without one, the runs are the natural runs; the distribution is balanced.

natural-merge.name: Natural Merge
natural-merge.tagline: Merge the runs that are already there
natural-merge.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n log n) · ✓ | 1495 sim GOOD | 10165 sim PASS | 4 | 6 | ~150 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Find the ascending runs in A. Merge them in pairs: push the first run to B,
then merge both smallest first onto A's bottom. A value of the second run is already on A's
top (`ra`); a value of the first is at B's bottom (`rrb pa ra`). The merged run ends up behind
the runs not yet merged, so the next pair is on top. Repeat passes until one run is left.

**Lore.** This is the natural merge sort of the tape era, and the core of Timsort (Tim Peters,
2002), Python's and Java's sort for objects: real data has runs, so merge them instead of
starting from scratch.

**Pros**
- A clean O(n log n) proof: ⌈log₂ runs⌉ passes, at most 4 ops per value per pass.
- Sorted input is free.

**Cons**
- **It is the lesson card for this model.** Every pass rotates all of A, even when only two
  runs need merging, so nearly sorted input is not cheap: one random swap at n=100 costs 454,
  against 106 for Long Line (sim). Timsort's trick depends on cheap random access to the runs,
  which stacks do not have.
- Random input has about n/2 runs, so it is the most expensive n log n card: 1495 / 10165, and
  its worst random run at n=500 (11791) is close to the PASS limit.

**Slots:** none.

lookahead-greedy.name: Lookahead Greedy
lookahead-greedy.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | Speed | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(n²·bᵏ) CPU · heuristic | 557 sim EXC | 5284 sim EXC | 6 | 6 | ~300 | ●●○○○ | Rare |

**How it plays.** Turk, but instead of taking the single cheapest move, evaluate the best
**sequence** of k moves (for example k = 2: the cost of this move plus the cheapest next move
after it). Only consider the top b candidates per level to bound the CPU cost.

The sim measures k = 2 among the 10 cheapest moves, re-planning after every move.

**Lore.** Lookahead is the oldest idea in game-playing programs: Shannon's 1950 chess paper
already proposed looking a few moves ahead. Here it turns out not to help (see the card), which
is itself the lesson.

**Pros**
- Built on Turk's code, so it is a short step from it.
- The idea is right: Turk's short-sightedness does cost ops, as Beam over Orders shows on LIS
  Insertion.

**Cons**
- **It is not an upgrade.** At n=100 it ties Turk (557); at n=500 it is worse, 5284 against
  5088, and only 96.5 % of its runs are EXCELLENT (sim). Re-planning every move, it keeps
  paying now for a cheap next move it then never takes. Committing to both moves halves the
  loss (+88 at n=500) but does not turn it into a gain.
- CPU grows with bᵏ.

**Slots:** 2, from anchor and band. The lookahead pick and its pricing are native, and it has
no order role: the lookahead already searches over the next moves. Defaults as Turk: Keep
Three and Hardcoded Three.

beam-sorter.name: Beam Sorter
beam-sorter.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | Speed | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| heuristic | 503 exp EXC | 4562 exp EXC | 10 | 10 | ~600 | ●○○○○ | Legendary |

**How it plays.** Keep the W best partial solutions (the beam). At each step, expand each
partial solution by the useful next moves, score every candidate with (ops so far + heuristic
estimate of the remaining cost), and keep the top W. The heuristic can be a **pattern
database**: exact distances for small groups of ranks, summed. Applied to the whole problem,
the beam is too slow at 500, so the strongest reference build uses it **inside** other cards:
for leaves of up to ~32 values and for choosing insertion orders.

**As built (exp).** The explorer's Beam Sorter searches whole insertion plans on the Insertion
bench (LIS kept, `rb` Sink in pass 1): W = 64 plans, each expanded by its 4 cheapest next
insertions, scored by ops so far plus h × (mean cheapest cost of the values left) × √(values
left), with h = 0.25. It measures 503 at n=100, the best single card at that size, but 4562 at
n=500, worse than Long Line's 4425, and it takes about 26 s per sort there in JS (exp). That keeps
the verdict: a whole-problem beam pays at n=100 and is the wrong tool at n=500.

**Lore.** Beam search comes from speech recognition: Bruce Lowerre's Harpy system (1976) kept
only the best few hypotheses at each step to stay fast. Pattern databases come from puzzle
solving (Culberson and Schaeffer, mid-1990s): precompute exact costs for small parts and use
them as estimates. They are what later made optimal Rubik's Cube solving possible.

**Pros**
- The strongest known results come from search layered on a structured algorithm. The
  reference build that uses it inside Four-End Quicksort averages 420 / 3111 on that method
  (ref, 5 seeds).
- One knob, W, trades CPU for ops.

**Cons**
- The Grasp and Craft limits of the deck: hashing, memory limits, heuristics, a time budget.
- Hard to justify as "one method" in the README. The subject wants a stated complexity class.

**Slots:** none. Params: the beam width W and the heuristic. Inside other cards, the same
search plays as Beam Leaf (a Finisher) and Beam over Orders (order).

annealer.name: Annealer
annealer.doc:
| class | @100 | @500 | Grasp | Craft | Lines | Speed | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| heuristic | 575 exp EXC | 5060 exp EXC | 8 | 6 | ~200 | ●○○○○ | Legendary |

**How it plays.** Simulated annealing over a **plan**, not over raw ops. The plan can be the
insertion order (LIS Insertion), the chunk boundaries (Chunks), or the pivots (quicksort). Make
a small random change, re-simulate, and keep the change if it is better (or occasionally if it
is worse, with a probability that falls over time).

**Lore.** Simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi, 1983) copies how metal cools:
early on, accept bad moves often, so the search can escape local optima; later, almost never.

**Pros**
- Works with any card that has a plan to tweak.
- Easy to bolt on top of an existing build.

**Cons**
- Not deterministic unless seeded.
- Each candidate needs a full re-simulation, which is slow.
- **As built (exp):** annealing over the chunk boundaries of Crate Runner (Chunks with One-Way
  Sweep and Second-Max), 400 trials: 575 / 5060 against Crate Runner's 607 / 5226. About
  0.1 s per sort at n=100 and 3 s at n=500 in JS. The gain is real but small: plans are
  cheap to perturb, and the boundaries barely matter once the sweep and retrieval are good.

**Slots:** none. Param: what to perturb. Inside another card, the same idea plays as the
Annealed Plan technique (order).

rank-compression.name: Rank Compression
rank-compression.tagline: Forget the values, keep the order
rank-compression.effect: enables most cards; 0 ops by itself
rank-compression.doc:
Replace each value with its rank 0..n−1. This can be done with a merge sort in O(n log n),
which also detects duplicates (equal neighbours) and counts inversions for free.

- **Pros:** Radix needs it. Chunks and buckets become arithmetic. It removes INT_MIN/INT_MAX
  edge cases from the algorithm code.
- **Cons:** none for ops. The O(n²) counting version is slow but fine at n=500.
- **Hosts:** all cards. It is always on in the explorer and shown in the input panel. The
  Codex keeps it as a card so peers learn that it is a choice.

presorted-shortcut.name: Presorted Shortcut
presorted-shortcut.effect: sorted input → 0; a rotation by k → min(k, n − k)
presorted-shortcut.doc:
If A is already sorted, output nothing. If A is a **rotation** of the sorted order, output
only the shorter rotation. Optionally, if it is sorted except for the top two, output `sa`.

- **Measured:** on sorted input, bare cards spend from 0 (Long Line, Quick 2-Way) up to 1084 at
  n=100 (LSD Radix) and 3914 at n=500 (Four-End Quicksort); on a sorted input rotated by n/4,
  every card pays 175 to 1084 ops at n=100, against 25 for the shortcut (sim).
- **Pros:** free, and the subject requires the no-op output for sorted input.
- **Cons:** only helps on special inputs: it never fires on uniform random input.
- **Hosts:** all cards.

disorder-meter.name: Disorder Meter
disorder-meter.effect: none on its own: it feeds the Adaptive Selector
disorder-meter.doc:
Disorder = inversions ÷ (n(n−1)/2), as the subject defines it, computed with a merge-sort
count in O(n log n). Alternatives are runs, LIS deficit and displacement (see the Adaptive
Selector).

- **Pros:** required for `--adaptive` and `--bench`.
- **Cons:** the inversion ratio is a poor predictor for some cards. For example, a rotated
  sorted input has high disorder but is nearly free.
- **Hosts:** the Adaptive Selector.

lis-anchor.name: LIS Anchor
lis-anchor.doc:
Keep a longest increasing subsequence, found by patience sorting with predecessor links in
O(n log n). The expected LIS of a random permutation approaches 2√n, but it is shorter at
these sizes: about 17 values at n=100 and 40 at n=500 (sim).

- **Measured:** on Simple Insertion, −65 at n=100 (1462 → 1397) and −366 at n=500 (sim). With
  Cheapest Pick added, it is the bare LIS Insertion card (547). The two overlap: Cheapest Pick
  alone takes Simple Insertion to 588, so the anchor adds only −41 on top of it.
- **Pros:** optimal for its job: the fewest pushes possible while keeping A ordered.
- **Cons:** pass 1 must still `ra` past the kept values, so each one costs a rotation instead
  of two pushes. The saving is smaller than "2 per kept value".
- **On Turk:** keeping the LIS instead of three values gives −9 at n=100 but **+49** at n=500
  (sim). Turk's cheapest pick already avoids most of what the anchor saves, and the kept values
  sit between the ones it still has to push.
- **Hosts:** Simple Insertion, Turk (replacing Keep Three), Insert-into-B (mirrored).
- **Conflicts:** other anchors.

circular-lis-anchor.name: Circular LIS Anchor
circular-lis-anchor.doc:
A is a circle, so the kept set only needs to be increasing **circularly**. Take the best LIS
over all n rotations (O(n² log n)).

- **Measured:** on LIS Insertion (Four-Way Cost, one band), −6 ± 1 at n=100, −7 ± 4 at n=200
  and −17 ± 11 at n=500 (sim). The anchor is about 2 values longer at n=100 and 4 at n=500.
  An earlier run reported +15 at n=500 from 40 inputs, which was within its noise.
- **On Turk:** −13 at n=100 and +45 at n=500 instead of Keep Three (sim), like LIS Anchor.
- **Pros:** never shorter than the plain LIS.
- **Cons:** a small gain for an O(n² log n) search over rotations. Keeping more values does not
  save much, because each kept value still costs a rotation in pass 1.
- **Hosts:** as LIS Anchor.

longest-run-anchor.name: Longest Run Anchor
longest-run-anchor.tagline: Keep the longest contiguous ordered block
longest-run-anchor.effect: Simple Insertion + Cheapest Pick −7 @100, −20 @500; on Turk +20 / +83
longest-run-anchor.doc:
Keep the longest stretch of **adjacent** values that are already in order. It is trivial to
find in O(n).

- **Measured:** on Simple Insertion + Cheapest Pick, −7 at n=100 and −20 ± 12 at n=500; on Turk
  instead of Keep Three, +20 / +83 (sim).
- **Pros:** very easy. It is free on nearly sorted inputs.
- **Cons:** on random input the longest run is short, about 5 values at n=100–500 (sim), so
  the effect is small, and on Turk it is negative.
- **Hosts:** as LIS Anchor.

keep-three.name: Keep Three
keep-three.tagline: Leave three, sort them by hand
keep-three.doc:
Stop pushing when 3 values remain in A and sort them with Hardcoded Three.

- **Pros:** Turk's default anchor, and native in Min Extract. Zero Grasp cost.
- **Cons:** it keeps only 3, against ~2√n for the LIS.
- **Hosts:** Turk, Min Extract.

cheapest-pick.name: Cheapest Pick
cheapest-pick.effect: LIS host −850 @100 (1397 → 547); alone on Simple Insertion −874
cheapest-pick.doc:
Instead of taking the top of the source stack, evaluate every value in it and move the one
whose total rotation cost is lowest.

- **Measured:** on an LIS-anchored Simple Insertion, 1397 → 547 at n=100 (−850) and −26,817 at
  n=500 (sim). Alone, without the anchor, it takes Simple Insertion from 1462 to 588. This is
  the largest single technique effect in the deck.
- **Pros:** turns O(n²) blind insertion into an EXCELLENT-grade card.
- **Cons:** O(n) candidates per move, each needing a slot lookup. That is O(n³) CPU per sort
  with a linear slot search, and O(n² log n) with a binary search, since A is circularly
  sorted. Both are fine at 500: the sim's linear version takes about 45 ms per sort.
- **Param: the candidate window.** Only the w values nearest either end of the source stack
  are priced. On Turk, w = 20 gives the same ops at n=100 and +65 at n=500, w = 50 the same at
  both, w = 5 costs +23 / +2658 (sim). The best move is almost always near an end, so the window
  cuts CPU from O(n) candidates per move to 2w. It does not change the class.
- **Hosts:** Simple Insertion, Insert-into-B. It is native in Turk and LIS Insertion.
- **Requires:** a cost card (it defaults to Two-Way Cost).

two-way-cost.name: Two-Way Cost
two-way-cost.doc:
Price each stack independently by its shorter direction. If both directions agree, the cost
is max(a, b), because `rr`/`rrr` move both stacks at once; otherwise it is a + b.

- **Pros:** simple.
- **Cons:** it misses the case where going the **longer** way on one stack lets both stacks
  share rotations.
- **Hosts:** any card with Cheapest Pick.

four-way-cost.name: Four-Way Cost
four-way-cost.doc:
Price `rr` (max(fa, fb)), `rrr` (max(ba, bb)), `ra+rrb` (fa + bb) and `rra+rb` (ba + fb), and
take the minimum.

- **Measured:** on LIS Insertion, −4 at n=100, −9 at n=200 and −19 at n=500, and the same on
  Turk, −4 / −19 (sim). A reference build rejected it as not worth the code. Turk peers usually
  include it.
- **Pros:** per move it is never worse than Two-Way Cost, because Two-Way's choice is one of
  its four. About ten extra lines.
- **Cons:** a small gain, and not a guaranteed one. A cheaper move now can leave a worse
  layout, so over a whole sort Four-Way ends worse than Two-Way on 11 % of inputs at n=100
  and 17 % at n=500 (sim).
- **Conflicts:** Two-Way Cost.

lookahead-k.name: Lookahead-k
lookahead-k.doc:
Score a candidate by its cost plus the cheapest follow-up move after it (depth k, keeping the
top-b candidates).

- **Measured (k = 2):** it makes things **worse**. Among the 3 cheapest moves: Turk −2 at n=100
  but +175 at n=500, Long Line +25 / +297; among the 10 cheapest it is no better (sim).
- **Why it loses:** it re-plans after every move, so it keeps paying extra now for a cheap
  follow-up it then never takes. Committing to both moves of the best pair halves the loss at
  n=500 (+88 instead of +175), but it is still worse than the plain greedy (sim). Beam over Orders, which compares
  whole partial plans, is the version that gains.
- **Cons:** CPU grows with bᵏ.
- **Hosts:** Turk, LIS Insertion, Bucket Insertion.

rb-sink.name: `rb` Sink (Two Bands)
rb-sink.doc:
Role: band. Right after pushing a value from the lower half of its range, `rb` it to the bottom
of B. B becomes two bands (an "hourglass"): high values near the top, low values near the
bottom. When the next op is an `ra`, the `rb` merges into one `rr`.

- **Measured:** on LIS Insertion, −14 at n=100, −93 at n=200 and −616 at n=500 (sim). The
  effect grows with n. The split point is a param: sinking below 0.4·n or 0.5·n is best, and
  0.7·n costs +23 / +222 (sim).
- **Pros:** cheap to add. Retrieval rotations shorten because B is roughly ordered.
- **Cons:** an extra `rb` per sunk value, unless it pairs with an `ra`.
- **Hosts:** Chunks and Bucket Insertion (default), Butterfly (through its window rule),
  Simple Insertion, LIS Insertion, Turk (variant).

multi-band.name: Multi-Band
multi-band.doc:
Role: band. Generalise to k bands, using both the top and bottom of B with a split per band.

- **Not buildable as written:** B has only two cheap ends, so a third band has nowhere to go
  without rotating past the others. Its measurable part is the split point of `rb` Sink, which
  is a param of that card (see above). Proposal: drop this card, or make it the split param.
- **Pros:** B is closer to sorted before retrieval.
- **Cons:** more bookkeeping.

sb-seed.name: `sb` Seed
sb-seed.effect: Turk +0.3: the sb costs more than it saves
sb-seed.doc:
Role: band. After Turk's opening `pb pb`, `sb` if needed so the two seeds are in descending
order.

- **Measured:** +0.3 on Turk at both sizes (sim): the `sb` it sometimes spends is not won back.
- **Pros:** one op, and slightly better early targets.
- **Cons:** a net loss, however small.
- **Hosts:** Turk.

middle-out-push.name: Middle-Out Push
middle-out-push.doc:
Role: band. Push the chunks from the middle outwards: chunks above the middle go on top of B,
chunks below it are sunk. B ends up sorted chunk by chunk, from the highest at the top to the
lowest at the bottom.

- **Measured:** instead of `rb` Sink on Chunks, +141 at n=100 and +1794 at n=500 (sim). The push
  phase costs the same; the whole loss is in retrieval.
- **Why it loses:** `rb` Sink splits each chunk across B's top and bottom, so max retrieval only
  searches half a chunk in either direction. Here each chunk sits whole on one side, so
  retrieval searches all of it.
- **Hosts:** Chunks.

nearest-member-sweep.name: Nearest-Member Sweep
nearest-member-sweep.doc:
Role: sweep. When pushing a chunk, bring the **nearest** member of the chunk to the top,
searching both directions, instead of rotating `ra` until one appears.

- **Pros:** none measured. It looks smarter than a blind `ra` sweep, but on Chunks it costs
  16 more ops at n=100 and 140 more at n=500 (sim).
- **Why it loses:** an `ra` sweep gets every member for free, because each `pb` takes the top
  value and so moves the sweep forward. An `rra` sweep pays one `rra` for every value it pulls
  up, members included. Picking the nearest member by distance alone ignores that.
- **Cons:** it can pass the same value many times, which weakens the O(n√n) proof.
- **Hosts:** Chunks (default), Bucket Insertion (with a caveat: it breaks the proof).

one-way-sweep.name: One-Way Sweep
one-way-sweep.effect: Chunks −16 @100, −140 @500 vs Nearest-Member; gives the n√n proof
one-way-sweep.doc:
Role: sweep. Per chunk, pick a direction and sweep once, never reversing. Price the two
directions honestly: an `ra` sweep pays only for the non-members it passes, while an `rra`
sweep pays for every value it pulls up, members included. So `ra` nearly always wins.

- **Pros:** gives a clean O(n√n) argument, because each chunk pass costs ≤ n. It is also the
  cheapest sweep measured: −16 at n=100 and −140 at n=500 against Nearest-Member on Chunks
  (sim).
- **Cons:** priced by distance alone, without the `rra` surcharge, it picks `rra` too often,
  loses that edge and ties Nearest-Member.
- **Hosts:** Bucket Insertion (default), Chunks.

max-retrieval.name: Max Retrieval
max-retrieval.doc:
Bring B's maximum to the top by the shorter direction and `pa`. Repeat.

- **Pros:** trivially correct. A ends up sorted with no final rotation.
- **Cons:** blind. It pays the full distance to every max.

second-max-lookahead.name: Second-Max Lookahead
second-max-lookahead.tagline: Grab the runner-up on the way
second-max-lookahead.doc:
If the second-largest value is cheaper to reach than the largest (by more than ~2 ops),
`pa` it first, then `pa` the max, then `sa`.

- **Pros:** a few lines, with a steady saving of about 3–6.5 %: −26 at n=100 and −385 at
  n=500 on Chunks, and −19 / −279 on Butterfly (sim).
- **Cons:** adds `sa` ops. It needs a threshold.
- **Requires:** a host whose default retrieval is Max Retrieval. It replaces Max Retrieval in
  the retrieval role and keeps its logic.

rank-range-max.name: Rank-Range Max
rank-range-max.effect: 0 by construction: a correctness and CPU fix
rank-range-max.doc:
Search for the max **by rank range** (for example, "the next expected rank") rather than by
scanning. It also fixes the bug of assuming a chunk stays contiguous in B.

- **Measured:** 0 by construction: it finds the same max as Max Retrieval.
- **Pros:** correctness and CPU.
- **Cons:** no ops gained.

cheapest-return.name: Cheapest Return
cheapest-return.doc:
Instead of the max, pick the B value (optionally restricted to the current bucket) whose
B rotation plus A slot rotation is cheapest, and insert it into A's circular order. Finish by
rotating the minimum to the top.

- **Measured:** on Chunks, +21 at n=100 but −494 at n=500; restricted to the top bucket, +38 /
  −541 (sim). It pays off at n=500 only.
- **Pros:** the biggest retrieval upgrade at n=500. It turns Chunks into Bucket Insertion.
- **Cons:** brings in Turk's complexity, and it is worse than Max Retrieval at n=100.
  Restricting it to one bucket is needed to keep the O(n√n) proof.
- **Conflicts:** Max Retrieval.

four-ends.name: Four Ends
four-ends.doc:
Role: ends. Use the top and bottom of both stacks as four destinations. A part sent to the
bottom of the current stack costs one rotation and never needs restoring.

- **Measured:** on Quick 2-Way with halves, both with 2-value leaves: +6 at n=100 and −355 at
  n=500 (sim).
- **Pros:** removes the "undo the rotations" overhead of Quick 2-Way. This is the key idea of
  Four-End Quicksort.
- **Cons:** direction logic depends on which end a chunk sits at. Only the max part may go to
  the top of A, because sorted output piles up there.

restore-skip.name: Restore Skip
restore-skip.effect: the whole-stack case is in the bare Quick 2-Way (−139 / −732 vs always restoring)
restore-skip.doc:
Role: ends, as a variant of Quick 2-Way's two ends. In Quick 2-Way, skip the `rra` restore
when the chunk is the whole stack, or when the remaining part can be processed from the
bottom instead. The first case is part of the bare Quick 2-Way: always restoring would cost
+139 at n=100 and +732 at n=500 (sim). The second case is not built in the sim; carried
through, it becomes Four Ends.

- **Pros:** an easy saving.
- **Cons:** many special cases.

thirds-split.name: Thirds Split
thirds-split.doc:
Role: split. Split by two pivots into low, mid and high parts, and send each to a different
place.

- **Measured:** with Four Ends and no Finisher, −86 at n=100 and −330 at n=500 against halves
  (sim).
- **Pros:** recursion depth log₃ n. Fewer passes over each value.
- **Cons:** needs at least three destinations. That is natural with Four Ends, awkward
  without.
- **Requires:** Four Ends, or a host with a third destination. **Conflicts:** Median Pivot,
  which cuts into two.

dp-splits.name: DP Splits
dp-splits.effect: vs Pivot by Leaf Count, BFS Leaf ≤ 5: −17 @100, −214 @500
dp-splits.doc:
Role: split. A dynamic program over (chunk size, location, whether the stacks hold other
values) chooses part sizes and destinations that minimise the **expected** op count. It
includes `rr` merges and free cases, such as a chunk alone on its stack.

- **Measured (sim, simplified):** a DP over (size, end) using per-value move costs and the BFS
  leaves' average costs, without `rr` merges or free reads. Instead of Pivot by Leaf Count, with
  BFS Leaf ≤ 5: −17 at n=100 and −214 at n=500.
- **Measured (ref):** the build that uses the full DP, together with beam leaves, averages 3111
  at n=500 on its complex method, against 3824 for the reference Four-End Quicksort without
  them (5 seeds).
- **Pros:** the strongest partition card.
- **Cons:** Legendary Grasp. It needs measured leaf costs as input.
- **Requires:** Four Ends. **Conflicts:** Median Pivot and Pivot by Leaf Count, because it
  chooses the part sizes itself.

median-pivot.name: Median Pivot
median-pivot.doc:
Role: pivot. Split at the median rank of the chunk, into two halves. Ranks make the median
exact and free.

- **Pros:** balanced recursion with depth log₂ n.
- **Cons:** two parts only, so many passes.

pivot-by-leaf-count.name: Pivot by Leaf Count
pivot-by-leaf-count.doc:
Role: pivot. Choose pivots so that the final leaves come out full (for example, ⌈m/5⌉ leaves of
up to 5 values), instead of splitting in equal thirds.

- **Measured:** with BFS Leaf ≤ 5, −27 at n=100 and −334 at n=500; without a Finisher, +12 /
  −89 (sim). Together with BFS Leaf it is a **synergy**: the pair saves 39 / 245 more than the
  two alone add up to.
- **Pros:** fewer wasted small leaves. Pairs with BFS Leaf.
- **Cons:** more arithmetic, and on its own it barely helps.

beam-over-orders.name: Beam over Orders
beam-over-orders.doc:
Keep the W best partial insertion orders, expanding each by the cheapest few next insertions,
and score them by ops so far. Width can be scaled by size, for example W = budget ÷ b².

- **Measured:** on Long Line, keeping the 3 cheapest next insertions per order: W = 4 gives −7
  at n=100, W = 16 −14 and W = 64 −19. At n=500 it is about −46 ± 30 with W = 16–64, from 40
  inputs (sim). Unlike Lookahead-k, it gains, because it compares whole partial plans.
- **Measured (ref):** one reference build uses it in its medium method (√n buckets,
  488 / 3394) and its simple method (LIS insertion, 471 / 4312).
- **Pros:** fixes greedy regret systematically.
- **Cons:** CPU cost, and Legendary Craft.
- **Hosts:** LIS Insertion, Bucket Insertion, Turk.

annealed-plan.name: Annealed Plan
annealed-plan.doc:
Simulated annealing over a plan: insertion order, chunk boundaries or pivots. See the Annealer
card.

- **Measured:** over the chunk boundaries of Chunks, 200 trials per input: −47 at n=100 and −263
  at n=500 (sim). Each trial re-runs the whole card.
- **No fixed schedule hides in it:** averaged over inputs, the boundaries it settles on are
  equal widths, and reusing that average as a fixed schedule saves only 2 / 8 (sim). The gain
  is per input, so the search has to run at runtime.
- **Pros:** works with any host that has a plan.
- **Cons:** needs seeding to be deterministic, and CPU grows with the number of trials.

five-hand.name: Five Hand
five-hand.effect: good, not optimal: up to 6 more than the Oracle at 5
five-hand.doc: good. push two mins, Three, pull back

bfs-leaf.name: BFS Leaf (≤ 5)
bfs-leaf.doc: optimal. the rest of each stack is a fixed **wall** the search cannot touch. States pack into an integer key. On Four-End Quicksort: ≤ 3 saves 95 / 635, ≤ 5 saves 142 / 657 at n=100 / 500 (sim).

distance-tables.name: Distance Tables
distance-tables.effect: the same ops as BFS Leaf ≤ 4 (−105 / −657), only faster
distance-tables.doc: optimal, O(1) lookup. precomputed backward BFS from the goal. The same ops as BFS Leaf ≤ 4 (−105 / −657), only faster.

beam-leaf.name: Beam Leaf (≤ 32)
beam-leaf.doc: near optimal. pattern-database heuristic. Falls back to splitting if the beam result is too long. Not built in the sim (ref only).

double-op-sharing.name: Double-Op Sharing
double-op-sharing.doc:
When planning a move, emit `rr`/`rrr` for the shared part instead of separate `ra` and `rb`
ops. Cost cards assume it. Without it, the planner's prices are lies.

It is a **post** card that acts as each move is emitted, like No-op Suppression, and it is
always on. It is not a cost card, so it never competes with Two-Way or Four-Way Cost for the
cost role.

- **Measured:** switching it off costs Turk +98 at n=100 and +1224 at n=500, and Long Line
  +69 / +852 (sim). It is the biggest effect after Cheapest Pick itself.
- **Pros:** without it, Cheapest Pick saves much less.
- **Cons:** none. It is listed so peers notice that it is a choice.

noop-suppression.name: No-op Suppression
noop-suppression.effect: under 0.5 op per stream on every card
noop-suppression.doc:
Drop an op that changes nothing at the moment it is emitted: rotating or swapping a stack of
size < 2, or pushing from an empty stack. Record `rr` with one idle half as the single half.

- **Measured:** under 0.5 op per stream on every sim card: Long Line 0.4 (a sink with one value
  in B), Four-End Quicksort 0.4, Butterfly 0.05, the rest 0 (sim).
- **Pros:** makes every later rewrite an exact identity.
- **Cons:** none.

peephole-cancel.name: Peephole Cancel
peephole-cancel.doc:
Remove adjacent inverse pairs: `ra/rra`, `rb/rrb`, `rr/rrr`, `pa/pb`, `sa/sa`, `sb/sb`. Do it
in one left-to-right pass that treats the output as a stack, so cascades also cancel.

- **Measured:** on LSD Radix, −78 at n=100 and −55 at n=500: the `pb`s that end a pass are
  undone by the `pa`s that follow. Under one op on Turk and LIS hosts (sim): hosts that plan
  carefully leave little to cancel.

peephole-fuse.name: Peephole Fuse
peephole-fuse.effect: Chunks −17 / −106; Butterfly −20 / −166; with Cancel on Four-End Quicksort −33 / −217
peephole-fuse.doc:
Merge adjacent halves: `ra+rb → rr`, `rra+rrb → rrr`, `sa+sb → ss`.

- **Measured:** −17 at n=100 and −106 at n=500 on Chunks, and −20 / −166 on Butterfly, mostly
  a sunk value's `rb` meeting the next `ra`. Nothing on LSD Radix, which never rotates B, and
  under one op on Turk and LIS hosts, which already share rotations (sim). Together with
  Peephole Cancel on Four-End Quicksort: −33 / −217.

commutation-peephole.name: Commutation Peephole
commutation-peephole.effect: after Cancel + Fuse: ~0 on every card
commutation-peephole.doc:
Ops on different stacks commute. For example, `ra pb`… cannot be reordered, but `ra rb` can be
pulled together across an unrelated op on the other stack. Reorder within a window before
cancelling and fusing.

- **Measured:** after Cancel and Fuse, a window of 8 ops finds nothing more on any sim card
  except Four-End Quicksort, −0.15 at n=100 (sim). A reference build measured −0.4 and
  rejected it.
- **Lesson:** most of the value is already caught by the simple peephole.

portfolio.name: Portfolio
portfolio.tagline: Run them all, keep the shortest
portfolio.doc:
| cost | Grasp | Craft | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CPU × (number of hands) | 2 | 2 | Rare |

**How it plays.** Run every wrapped hand on a copy of the input and output the shortest stream.
The simplest version is "one band vs two bands" inside LIS Insertion: −8 ops at n=100 against
two bands alone, and nothing at n=500, where two bands always win (sim).

**Lore.** Huberman, Lukose and Hogg named algorithm portfolios in 1997 (in Science). They
borrowed the idea from finance: when no single method wins every input, spread the effort over
several and keep the best.

**Pros**
- Free ops. It can never be worse than its best member.

**Cons**
- An evaluator may not accept "the shortest of several streams" as **one method** for a
  complexity class. Its class is the worst of its members' classes.
- CPU multiplies.

adaptive-selector.name: Adaptive Selector
adaptive-selector.tagline: Read the table, pick the deck
adaptive-selector.doc:
| cost | Grasp | Craft | rarity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| one disorder measurement | 4 | 4 | Common (required by the subject's `--adaptive`) |

**How it plays.** Measure the input's disorder (inversions ÷ pairs, by the subject's
definition), then dispatch to a hand per range. The subject's baseline is < 0.2 → the O(n²)
hand, < 0.5 → the O(n√n) hand, and otherwise → the O(n log n) hand. These are also the
subject's class targets: whatever runs at disorder ≥ 0.5 must be O(n log n), and whatever
runs at 0.2–0.5 must be O(n√n) or better. In the Lab, the thresholds can be edited and drawn
on the Disorder map, so you can see whether the subject's cut points are where the hands
actually cross. Moving them flags any regime whose hand misses its class target.

**Uniform input sits on the cut.** The disorder of a uniform random input is 0.500 ± 0.034 at
n=100 and ± 0.015 at n=500, so about half of the evaluation's random inputs go to the medium
hand and half to the complex one (sim). The subject's own `--bench` example shows a random
500-value input at 49.93 % going to the O(n√n) method. A build's grade therefore depends on
both hands, and its worst runs come from the weaker one.

**Builds.** This card wrapped around a simple, a medium and a complex hand is a **build**: the
thing the evaluation actually runs. The Meta page ranks builds ([05-meta.md](../05-meta.md)).

**Variants (params):**
- **Metric choice:** inversions, runs, LIS deficit (n − LIS), displacement. Some metrics
  predict a card's cost better than others.
- **Predict, don't measure:** estimate each hand's cost from the metric with a fitted curve,
  instead of fixed thresholds.

**Lore.** Required by the subject; the disorder metric is the classic inversion count, which
measures how far a list is from sorted (it is also the number of swaps bubble sort needs).

**Pros**
- Required by the subject, and it makes "which card when?" explicit.

**Cons**
- With bad thresholds, it picks a worse hand than any single one would, or breaks a class
  target.
- The Disorder map makes both visible.

heapsort.name: Heapsort
heapsort.why: Sift-down jumps from i to 2i+1. The jumps along one sift-down double in length, so they add up to O(n) rotations, and n sift-downs cost O(n²) ops: quadratic, not n log n.

shell-sort.name: Shell sort
shell-sort.why: Gap comparisons need positions i and i+gap at the same time. With one swap op that only touches the top two, every gap compare costs about gap rotations, so the large-gap passes that make Shell sort fast are the most expensive here.

counting-sort.name: Counting sort
counting-sort.why: Ranks already give every value's final position. The hard part was never knowing where a value goes, only moving it there.
counting-sort.lesson: Rank Compression is the counting part.

pancake-sort.name: Pancake sort
pancake-sort.why: Its prefix reversal is a single operation there. Here, reversing k values costs about 2k ops (the optimum is 5, 9, 11 and 14 ops for k = 3 to 6).

sorting-networks.name: Bitonic / sorting networks
sorting-networks.why: Fixed compare-exchange pairs at arbitrary distances need random access.

bogosort.name: Bogosort
bogosort.why: Random shuffles. It is included as a joke and a lesson in expected cost.

cycle-sort.name: Cycle sort
cycle-sort.why: It minimises writes, but here moves are what cost, not writes. Following a cycle means rotating to each position.

merge-insertion.name: Merge insertion (Ford–Johnson)
merge-insertion.why: It sorts with the fewest comparisons known (1959), but push_swap counts moves, not comparisons.

smoothsort.name: Smoothsort / Cartesian tree sort
smoothsort.why: Adaptive in theory: nearly sorted input is cheap. But they keep a heap or tree over array positions, so they need random access, and they fall apart like heapsort.

stooge-sort.name: Stooge sort
stooge-sort.why: O(n^2.7) comparisons, made worse by rotations.

binary-indexed-tree.name: Binary indexed tree
binary-indexed-tree.why: It answers rank and position queries in O(log n) CPU. That speeds up a planner, for example Cheapest Pick's slot search, but it moves no values: the op count still comes from the method it serves.
